title: The Ultimate Checklist for Buying Used Heavy Equipment
summary: Learn how to buy used heavy equipment with confidence. Our inspection checklist and expert guidance help you make informed decisions. Contact us today.
body_text: Buying Used Heavy Equipment Ultimate Checklist Buying used heavy equipment is a great way to expand your fleet or replace older machines. The key is knowing exactly what to inspect in the equipment before you commit. After all, you’ll need a quality piece of equipment to avoid downtime and repairs. Follow our equipment inspection checklist to make more confident purchases. What to Do Before You Inspect the Machine The physical inspection is only half the battle when buying used heavy equipment. Before you ever lay eyes on the machine, follow these steps to position yourself for success: Define your specs and job requirements: Think like a fleet manager by defining the job the machine needs to accomplish. Know your required specifications, like lift capacity, engine power, GVWR and application-specific features, before you start shopping. This prevents you from overbuying capabilities you won’t use or underbuying power you’ll desperately need. Whether you’re considering specialized vocational trucks or tracked equipment, knowing your requirements helps you focus the search and negotiate from a position of knowledge. Know how to vet the seller: You can source your used equipment from different places, whether it’s a dealer, auction or private seller. The most important thing across all three sources is the seller’s ability to provide transparent, verifiable information about a machine’s history and condition. A reputable dealer who services what they sell offers a significant advantage — they can back up claims with maintenance records performed by their own technicians. Set a realistic budget beyond the sticker price: The total cost of ownership extends well beyond the purchase price. Budget for immediate costs like transport, taxes and insurance, as well as potential near-term expenses for tires, fluids or other wear parts. Always have a contingency fund for initial repairs or maintenance. When evaluating equipment like excavators, dozers and wheel loaders, factor in the operating costs specific to each machine type. Heavy Equipment Prepurchase Inspection Checklist Follow this used heavy equipment checklist to protect your investment and choose a top-quality machine: 1. Inspect the Frame and Structure for Cracks and Wear Start with a thorough walk-around of the entire machine. Look for signs of structural stress, especially around high-load areas, as well as fresh paint that could be hiding rust or previous repairs. Inspect all welds carefully, especially around booms, cranes and mounting points. Make sure the equipment doesn’t have any cracks, as these could mean it’s been stressed beyond its design limits. Examine the chassis for any bending or twisting that suggests the equipment has been in an accident or used improperly. Any inspection you perform should meet the federal structural integrity requirements outlined by the FMCSA. 2. Evaluate the Engine, Power Train and Exhaust The engine can tell you a lot about how the machine was operated. Check for oil leaks around seals, gaskets and the oil pan. Listen closely during a cold start for any strange sounds, such as knocking, which could indicate worn bearings. Remove the oil fill cap while the engine is running and check for excessive blowby, which suggests worn piston rings or cylinder walls. Note the color of exhaust smoke, as different colors indicate specific engine problems. Blue may mean burning oil, white suggests coolant in the combustion chamber, and black points to fuel system problems. Test the transmission through all gears and note how the machine shifts under load. 3. Test the Hydraulic System for Leaks and Performance For vocational trucks and heavy equipment, a well-functioning hydraulic system is essential. Check all the hoses for brittleness, cracks, and signs of previous repairs. Look for leaks around hydraulic cylinders, pumps, and fittings. Operate the equipment under a light load to test for hydraulic drift, where a raised implement slowly lowers on its own. This indicates worn seals or valves. Hydraulic fluid levels and condition show you whether the system is in good shape. 4. Check All Cab Controls and Electrical Systems Get in the cab and test every single component. Make sure every light works, every gauge responds accurately, and every switch functions as designed. Test the PTO engagement if applicable. A faulty electrical system can be difficult and expensive to diagnose and repair, so thorough testing now will save you from trouble later on. Check the condition of wiring harnesses for signs of rodent damage or previous amateur repairs. 5. Examine the Undercarriage, Tires or Tracks For wheeled equipment, check for uneven tire wear patterns, as these usually indicate alignment or suspension issues. Measure tread depth and check for sidewall damage. For tracked equipment, examine the sprockets, idlers, and the track itself for signs of wear, cracks, and missing components. An undercarriage replacement will be a major expense, so make sure these components are in good condition to help calculate your true acquisition cost. How to Verify the Equipment’s True History Documentation is just as important as your physical inspection. Knowing how to buy used heavy equipment means understanding service records, as these will tell you the true story of how equipment was treated during its working life: Review the service history: A quality service history shows consistent, preventive maintenance rather than just reactive repairs. Look for regular fluid changes, scheduled inspections and proactive component replacements. This documentation can prove that the previous owner invested in the machine’s longevity. Equipment maintained by expert technicians will usually come with detailed records, so you can be more confident in the machine’s condition. Know the difference between high hours and hard hours: An hour meter doesn’t tell the full story about a machine’s condition. A truck with high highway miles might be in much better shape than a low-hour unit that spent its entire life in severe-duty applications. Consider engine idle time versus PTO hours. Idle hours significantly impact engine wear , so you’ll need to factor them into the used equipment valuation. A machine with an auxiliary power unit might show high hours but less actual engine stress. Confirm you’re getting a clean title with no liens: Always run a formal lien check on any equipment you’re considering purchasing. This ensures the seller has the legal right to transfer ownership and that you won’t inherit outstanding debts attached to the machine. A clean title protects your investment from future legal complications. When you partner with a reputable company like Custom Truck One Source, you can rely on our expertise to handle the verification process for you. We know what to look for in service records because we’ve maintained these machines ourselves. Find a Work-Ready Unit With Custom Truck One Source When you’re ready to invest in reliable, work-ready equipment, turn to Custom Truck One Source for a solution built on transparency and quality. Much of our inventory comes from our own rental fleet, so you get verifiable service histories maintained by our technicians. Each unit undergoes a rigorous inspection process to meet performance and compliance standards before it reaches your operation. title: Pitney Bowes among the top 3 workplaces in India
body_text: Pitney Bowes has been named one of India’s Top 3 Great Mid-Size Workplaces For 2024 by the Great Place to Work®️ Institute. The announcement was made on June 20 at a ceremony in Mumbai and members of the Pitney Bowes India team were there to receive this prestigious award. Pitney Bowes joins the list for the 11th time alongside industry leaders. “Our commitment to excellence, inclusion, and trust has brought us here, and it will propel us forward. Each one of our employees plays an important role in shaping our culture and contributes to making us a great place to work every single day.” – Pankaj Sachdeva, Vice President Data Science & Analytics and Managing Director, Innovation. Pitney Bowes ranked 3 in the largest workplace culture study in the country. It is a matter of pride to be consistently recognized for our people-first culture. Pitney Bowes has earned this recognition for creating a Great Place to Work FOR ALL employees and has excelled on the 5 dimensions of building a High-Trust, High-Performance Culture™ – Credibility, Respect, Fairness, Pride, and Camaraderie. In 2024, Pitney Bowes was also named India’s Best Organizations for Women - 2024 by ET Now, a division of The Economic Times, one of India’s leading business publications. We were also recognized as one of India’s Top 25 Best WorkplacesTM Building a Culture of Innovation by All 2024 - Mid-size and India’s Top 50 Best WorkplacesTM in Health and Wellness 2023 by the Great Place to Work® Institute for fostering a holistic approach to employee health and wellbeing and for our industry-best innovation and people practices, respectively. Together, we continue to create an environment where everyone feels valued, thrives, and contributes to our shared success. To learn more about Life at Pitney Bowes visit pitneybowes.com/careers .

title: How to Set Up a Trust: A Comprehensive Guide for 2026
summary: Online and do-it-yourself options walk you through how to set up a trust. Revocable trust, irrevocable trust, living trust, or testamentary trust, all options are available to people from all economic strata.
body_text: FAQs on how to set up a trust 1. How do I transfer ownership of my house to my trust? To transfer ownership of your house to a trust, you need to create the trust and then: Draft a new deed transferring ownership to the trust. File it with the appropriate local office responsible for property records, such as the county clerk, recorder of deeds, or land records office, depending on your state or jurisdiction 2. How does the trust management and administration function? Trust management and administration involve carrying out the grantor's directives, managing assets, and distributing funds to beneficiaries. Trustees are responsible for overseeing the trust assets, ensuring the trust is conducted appropriately, monitoring expenses, accounting for and reporting on trust assets, and preparing tax and regulatory filings. Trustees receive hourly compensation for their work, while the costs tied to trust management and administration can fluctuate depending on the trust's complexity and the beneficiaries' requirements. Ongoing trust management during incapacity or after death is crucial to ensure the trust serves its intended purpose and provides financial security for your beneficiaries. 3. Can I make some legal arrangements to ensure my child graduates from college before certain other assets are distributed? Yes. When setting up a trust, you can ensure a beneficiary meets a certain age requirement before receiving assets. In this case, you could designate that all educational expenses would be paid at the university level. You can then designate that your child receive all or a portion of the assets you have set aside for the educational expenses of that individual. 4. How much money do you need to have trust? You can start a trust fund for as little as $100 in initial deposit and a few hundred dollars in fees, but if you have $100,000 or more and own real estate, then a trust might be beneficial. 5. What are the three primary types of trust? There are three primary classes of trusts: revocable trusts, irrevocable trusts, and testamentary trusts. A revocable trust can be altered or terminated during the trustor's lifetime, while an irrevocable trust cannot. Finally, a testamentary trust is created within the context of a will. 6. What is the difference between a revocable trust and an irrevocable trust? A revocable trust allows the grantor to make changes or terminate the trust. In contrast, an irrevocable trust is permanent and offers greater asset protection and potential tax benefits. 7. What are the ongoing taxes on trusts? If your trust has property that gains value, loses value, or otherwise creates income, you must pay the Internal Revenue Service taxes on that trust income on Form 1041 . When filing your state income tax returns, you'll want to check your state tax code to see if you need to file locally. 8. Can I set up an irrevocable trust for myself? Yes, you can set up an irrevocable trust for yourself. However, once it’s created, you generally give up control over the assets and can't make changes without court approval or beneficiary consent. People often use irrevocable trusts to protect assets or reduce estate taxes. 9. Can I withdraw money from a trust account? If you created a revocable trust, then yes. Only the trustee has the authority to withdraw money from a trust account, and even then, it must be done according to the trust's terms. If you’re a beneficiary, you can’t withdraw money yourself unless the trust document allows for direct access. 10. How do I access a trust fund? If you're a trust fund beneficiary, your access depends on the rules set by the grantor. Some trusts allow regular distributions, while others are tied to age milestones or specific events. Speak to the trustee to understand your rights. 11. What happens when a trust is formed? When a trust is formed, the trustee becomes responsible for managing any assets owned in the name of the Trust, and beneficiaries gain rights to distributions under the terms outlined in the trust document. 12. How to put assets in a trust? Funding a trust involves retitling property and updating account ownership. For example, to move a home into a trust, you’ll need to execute a new deed naming the trust as the property owner. For bank accounts, you’ll need to update the account title with your bank to reflect the trust’s name. This process varies slightly depending on the asset type and state laws, so it’s helpful to consult an estate attorney or financial institution. 13. Can I be both the trustee and the beneficiary of a trust? Yes, you can be both the trustee and a beneficiary, especially in a revocable trust. However, if it’s an irrevocable trust, dual roles may raise legal or tax complications, so it’s best to seek professional advice.

title: CAE to transfer U.S. stock exchange listing to Nasdaq
summary: /CNW/ - (NYSE: CAE) (TSX: CAE) – In line with the objectives of its transformation plan, CAE will voluntarily transfer its U.S. stock exchange listing from the...
body_text: MONTREAL , July 9, 2026 /CNW/ - (NYSE: CAE) (TSX: CAE ) – In line with the objectives of its transformation plan, CAE will voluntarily transfer its U.S. stock exchange listing from the New York Stock Exchange ("NYSE") to the Nasdaq Global Select Market ("Nasdaq"). The transition reflects CAE's continued focus on operational efficiency and aligning its market positioning with its profile as a global leader leveraging cutting-edge technology to deliver simulation, training and mission-critical solutions. CAE expects the last day of trading of its common shares on the NYSE to be Wednesday July 22, 2026, with trading on the Nasdaq expected to commence on Thursday, July 23, 2026. CAE's listing on the Toronto Stock Exchange ("TSX") will not be affected, and its common shares will continue to trade under the ticker symbol "CAE" on both the TSX and Nasdaq. title: From Transition to Transformation: A Site Move That Reflects How Collaboration Drives Progress
summary: By Hardy Gaschler, Director of Operations When we began the transition of injection molding operations from Ludwigsstadt, Germany, to our site in Sonneberg, Germany, the objective was clear. body_text: By Hardy Gaschler, Director of Operations When we began the transition of injection molding operations from Ludwigsstadt, Germany, to our site in Sonneberg, Germany, the objective was clear. The company needed to consolidate operations and improve efficiency. The reason for the move was straightforward. Continuing production in Ludwigsstadtis no longer practical. At the same time, Sonneberg has developed into experts in injection molding, making it the natural location for these operations. However, moving equipment is only one part of the story. The project required close coordination across multiple teams, including project leadership, manufacturing engineering, and planning. Weekly alignment meetings ensured that all stakeholders had a clear understanding of progress, risks, and priorities. One of the key challenges came from legacy constraints. In the past, tools were often dedicated to individual machines. This limited flexibility and made it more difficult to respond to increasing demand. As a result, the team needed to rethink how production capacity could be managed more effectively. The transition also highlighted the importance of investment in future capability. We are introducing new tools and considering additional machines. We are recreating clean room conditions in Sonneberg to meet production requirements. Although this project is primarily local, it reflects broader themes that are common in global organizations. Decisions about production and capacity are influenced by demand, supply chain considerations, and long-term strategy. This site move demonstrates how operational change and company culture are closely connected. The team is not only executing a transition. They are learning from past limitations and improving flexibility to prepare for future growth. The result will be more than a relocation. It will be a stronger and more resilient manufacturing operation. This is the Novanta Way in action.

About WSFS Financial Corporation WSFS Financial Corporation is a multibillion-dollar financial services company. Its primary subsidiary, WSFS Bank, is the oldest and largest locally headquartered bank and wealth management franchise in the Greater Philadelphia and Delaware region. As of March 31, 2026, WSFS Financial Corporation had $22.1 billion in assets on its balance sheet and $97.6 billion in assets under management and administration. WSFS operates from 114 offices, 87 of which are banking offices, located in Pennsylvania (58), Delaware (38), New Jersey (14), Florida (2), Nevada (1) and Virginia (1) and provides comprehensive financial services including commercial banking, consumer banking, treasury management, and trust and wealth management. Other subsidiaries or divisions include Arrow Land Transfer, Bryn Mawr Trust Advisors, LLC, Bryn Mawr Trust®, The Bryn Mawr Trust Company of Delaware, Cash Connect®, NewLane Finance®, WSFS Wealth® Management, LLC, WSFS Institutional Services®, and WSFS Mortgage®.
